newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New cosmonaut was "overcome by emotions" - doctor.
newsitem.headline: New cosmonaut was "overcome by emotions" - doctor.

text.p: Russia's novice relief cosmonaut, who holds the fate of the ailing Mir space station largely in his hands, was "overcome with emotions" during take-off, Mission Control's top doctor said on Wednesday.
Pavel Vinogradov, 43, a newcomer in space, will lead efforts to repair the troubled Mir after he arrives on Thursday. He and veteran commander Anatoly Solovyov blasted into orbit on Tuesday.
"Of course (Vinogradov) was worried, and perhaps he was to a certain extent overcome by emotions," Igor Goncharov, deputy flight director overseeing medical issues, told Reuters.
"Thus his pulse was somewhat higher than that of the experienced commander. We notice this in practically all new crew members flying for the first time," he added.
Goncharov said the first-time cosmonaut was now calmer.
"After entering orbit his pulse normalised," he said. "We talked to him today, he had no complaints, and feels great."

Solovyov, 49, is one of Russia's most experienced cosmonauts, with four missions to Mir and 456 days in space already under his belt. He and Vinogradov are due to link up with Mir at 1703 GMT on Thursday.

The new crew will inherit a ship which has run on partial power since the June 25 accident in which Mir's Spektr module collided with its resupply ship. Vinogradov will lead risky efforts to restore power on Mir and patch a puncture in Spektr, which is now sealed from the rest of the station.

He is also likely to face the task of repairing the Elektron oxygen generating system, which has not worked since last week. The crew aboard Mir continued efforts to fix it on Wednesday, but so far had not succeeded, officials said.
Mir's older back-up oxygen generator is not available for use because it is located in the Kvant-2 module, which the crew powered down to save energy after the collision.
"They are looking at using parts from the other Elektron unit on Kvant-2 and exchanging different units from that to the Elektron on Kvant-1," NASA spokeswoman Kathleen Maliga said.
The crew of two Russians and one American now on board Mir were relying on solid fuel oxygen generators called "candles" for their oxygen, officials said.

The current Mir crew of Vasily Tsibliyev, Alexander Lazutkin and British-born U.S. physicist Michael Foale prepared to welcome the new crew by undocking Mir's Progress cargo ship to create a parking space for their Soyuz craft.

The Progress T-35 delivered oxygen, food, water and tools to Mir on July 7. Now filled with garbage, it will orbit the Earth until the day after the current Russian crew returns home on August 14, Russian space officials said.

Yevgeny Shaposhnikov, adviser to President Boris Yeltsin on space and aviation, said Russia should continue to fund Mir as a training ground for the Alpha space station due to be assembled in stages by 2003.

"Mir is the base of the international space station which is called Alpha," he told reporters. "The station has considerable work experience, but nonetheless survives under these conditions, and overcomes all of these influences that arise.

"If it was stopped because of some holding back of pennies, let's say, we could lose millions and a very interesting international programme, since not a single country in the world has the experience we have," Shaposhnikov said.
